title: The servant's pledge and plea for guidance
tafsir:
Al-Fatihah has been speaking *about* Allah — praising Him, naming His mercy, acknowledging His ownership of the Day of Judgment. In ayah 5 the servant turns and speaks *to* Him: a pledge, and then, resting on that pledge, one request that runs to the end of the surah (ayat 6–7). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the last three verses of the surah consist of a prayer on man's part — that is, Allah Himself, in His great mercy, has taught man what to pray for.

## The turn to direct address

Ibn Kathir notices the grammar first. Until now Allah is spoken of in the third person; here the speech shifts to direct address with the *kāf* of *iyyāka* — "You" — because, having praised and thanked his Lord, the servant now stands before Him and addresses Him directly. Some of the Salaf said Al-Fatihah is the secret of the Qur'an and these words the secret of Al-Fatihah. Ibn Kathir explains why: the first half of ayah 5 is a declaration of innocence from *shirk* (associating anything with Allah), while the second negates having any power or strength of one's own, recognising that all affairs are controlled by Allah alone.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows how ayah 5 grows out of what precedes it. The opening ayat cover a life in time — the Lord of the worlds and the All-Merciful for man's past and present, "Master of the Day of Judgment" for his future, when he can have no helper but Allah. Once that dependence is clear in all three states, two conclusions follow of themselves: Allah alone deserves worship, and Allah alone is worth asking for help.

## "You alone" — how the Arabic says it

The word order carries the exclusivity. Arabic normally puts the object after the verb; here the object *iyyāka* ("You") comes first. Ibn Kathir reads it: we worship You alone and none else, and rely on You alone and none else — "this is the perfect form of obedience, and the entire religion is implied by these two ideas."

*ʿIbādah* (worship) rewards slowing down over. Linguistically, Ibn Kathir says, its sense is *being subdued* — a road is called *muʿabbadah*, meaning paved. In religious usage it implies the utmost love, humility and fear; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the decisive rider that such willing self-abasement cannot justly be adopted towards anyone except Allah.

Ibn Kathir adds that worship is named before help because worship is the objective while Allah's help is the tool for reaching it. And *nastaʿīn* ("we ask for help") names no particular need — a generality most commentators take as deliberate, covering acts of worship and every worldly and otherworldly concern.

## The conversation inside every prayer

Sahih Muslim records from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah says: "I divided the prayer into two halves between Myself and My servant, one half is for Me and one half for My servant. My servant shall have what he asks for." As the worshipper recites the opening ayat, Allah answers each in turn — "My servant has praised Me," "My servant has praised Me," "My servant has glorified Me." Then at ayah 5, "This is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked." And at ayat 6–7, "This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked."

Of the whole surah, ayah 5 is the one line Allah describes as *between* Himself and His servant. Ibn Kathir draws the practical lesson: this is the best method for seeking help — first praise the One from whom help is sought, then ask for His aid, for oneself and for one's Muslim brethren, by saying, "Guide us to the straight path."

## Why ask for guidance if you already have it?

A believer is already guided, the prophets and the righteous most of all — so why ask, in every unit of prayer, "Guide us"? Ibn Kathir answers that if it were not a fact that the believer needs to keep asking for guidance day and night, Allah would not have directed him to ask for it. The servant cannot benefit or harm himself except by Allah's permission, so ayah 6 means: "Make us firm on the path of guidance and do not allow us to deviate from it" — the spirit of "Our Lord! Let not our hearts deviate after You have guided us" (3:8). And the request is made in the plural, *ihdinā*, "guide **us**": one asks for oneself and for one's Muslim brethren at once.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers by opening up the word *hidāyah*, following Imam Raghib al-Isfahani: guidance is leading someone towards his destination gently and kindly, and it comes in degrees. The **first** is universal — every created thing is given its distinctive form and then guided to its function (20:50). The **second** is particular to rational beings, men and jinn, and reaches them through prophets and revealed books; some accept it, some reject it. The **third** is *tawfīq* — Allah's grace supplying the inward and outward means and circumstances that make it easy, even pleasant, to accept and act on guidance. Like the first, it descends directly from Allah, a prophet's role being confined to the second degree, and its scope is limitless: "As for those who follow the straight path, Allah will increase their guidance" (47:17). That is why even the greatest kept asking: Surah al-Fath counts "and to guide you on the straight path" (48:20) among the blessings named in the Prophet's ﷺ later days, when he was already guided and a source of guidance for others.

## What "straight" means

Ibn Kathir quotes Imam Abu Jaʿfar At-Tabari: the Ummah agreed that *as-sirāt al-mustaqīm* is the clear path without branches — the Arabs would describe the honest man as straight and the wicked man as crooked — and in the Qur'an it refers to Islam. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the sense of a road with no turns and twists: the particular way of faith that equally avoids the two extremes of excess and deficiency, so that in doctrine and practice both one neither goes beyond the limits nor falls short of them.

Imam Ahmad recorded in his Musnad from An-Nawwas bin Samʿan that the Prophet ﷺ gave this parable: a straight path surrounded by two walls on both sides, the walls set with open doors covered with curtains; a caller at the gate of the path crying, "O people! Stay on the path and do not deviate from it," and another caller from above warning anyone who wants to open one of those doors not to open it. The path, he ﷺ said, is Islam; the two walls are Allah's set limits; the doors are what Allah has prohibited; the caller at the gate is the Book of Allah; and the caller above is Allah's admonishment in the heart of every Muslim.

## Ayah 7: a path identified by the people who walked it

Ayah 7 defines that path, first positively. "Those upon whom You have bestowed Your grace," says Ibn Kathir, are those named in Surah An-Nisa': "the Prophets, the Siddiqin (the truly faithful), the martyrs, and the righteous" (4:69). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the four categories: the prophets are the greatest of them; the *Siddiqin* (the constantly true) are those who attain spiritual perfection and so hold the highest rank among a prophet's followers; the *Shuhadā* are those who sacrifice even their lives for their faith, or who bear witness to the truth, as the word admits both meanings; and the *Salihin* (the righteous) are those who follow the Shariah completely — not only in the matter of obligations but also in its commendable acts.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws something striking from this. It would have been shorter and more explicit to say "the path of the Qur'an" or "the path of the Prophet ﷺ" — yet two ayat of this short surah are spent pointing us to *people*, and among them to categories who will always be found living among us till the last day. A book alone is not enough for the grooming of man: "Courses teach words. But, men train men." So one who wants to understand the Book of Allah and act upon it cannot rely on his own study and judgment alone, but must turn to someone who knows — while assessing any such person against the well-known principles of the Book of Allah itself.

Then the path is marked out negatively, by the ditch on either side. Ibn Kathir: those who earned anger are those whose intentions are corrupt, "who know the truth, yet deviate from it"; those who went astray "lost the true knowledge and, as a result, are wandering in misguidance, unable to find the correct path." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān maps this onto deficiency and excess — the first are deficient in obeying divine injunctions, going against commandments they know perfectly well out of desire or calculated perversity; the second, out of ignorance or lack of thought, go beyond the limits Allah appointed and indulge in excess and exaggeration in religious matters.

As to who these were, Ibn Kathir cites the hadith Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAdi bin Hatim — who had been a Christian before he accepted Islam, and who came to the Prophet ﷺ and found women and children gathered so close about him that he knew this was no king like Kisra or Caesar — in which he ﷺ said, "Those who have earned the anger are the Jews and those who are led astray are the Christians." At-Tirmidhi also collected it and said it is *Hasan Gharib*. Ibn Kathir notes that both descriptions may touch either community, but anger is more particular to the Jews, who knew and abandoned practising, and straying to the Christians, who wanted the true knowledge but did not seek it from its proper sources. These, he says, are paths the believer should beware of, so that he avoids them.

## Saying Amin

Ibn Kathir writes that it is recommended to say "Amin" after finishing the recitation of Al-Fatihah: it means, "O Allah! Accept our invocation." Imams Ahmad, Abu Dawud and At-Tirmidhi recorded that Wa'il bin Hujr heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite the closing words of ayah 7 and say "Amin," extending it with his voice. At-Tirmidhi explained "Amin" as "Do not disappoint our hope"; the majority of scholars said it means "Answer our invocation." And Sahih Muslim records from Abu Musa that the Prophet ﷺ said, "When the Imam says *wa lad-dāllin*, say 'Amin' and Allah will answer your invocation."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical lesson from the surah's shape: begin by fulfilling your obligation to praise Allah; then offer the pledge that you regard no one but Allah as worthy of worship, and no one but Allah as having real power to help you in need; and only then ask for what you wish. And ask for something so comprehensive that it contains in essence every other human goal — as being guided on the straight path does, for one who keeps to it in everything, material or spiritual, need not fear stumbling.
